quote: For freedom Christ set us free; so stand firm.
firstReading: Paul proclaims that Christ has liberated believers from slavery and urges them not to submit again to a yoke of servitude. He warns the Galatians that seeking justification through circumcision binds them to the whole Law and separates them from the grace of Christ. In Christ, what matters is neither circumcision nor uncircumcision, but faith active through love.
psalmSummary: The psalmist pleads for the Lord’s merciful love and saving help according to God’s promise. He asks that the word of truth remain on his lips, because he hopes in the divine judgments. Keeping God’s law brings enduring fidelity, freedom of movement in obedience, delight in the commandments, and a loving lifting of hands toward the statutes of the Lord.
gospelSummary: When a Pharisee is surprised that Jesus does not perform the customary washing before a meal, Jesus exposes a false concern for outward cleanliness. He says that the Pharisees cleanse what is visible while their inner life is marked by greed and wickedness. The God who made the exterior also made the interior; therefore worship cannot be reduced to ritual appearance. Jesus calls for a generosity that reaches what is within, so that the whole person may be purified. His rebuke does not reject true reverence for God, but condemns religious practice that leaves the heart untouched and neglects mercy.
saintReflection: Saint Theophilus of Antioch (Commemoration): Saint Theophilus of Antioch was a second-century bishop and Christian apologist whose surviving work, addressed to Autolycus, explains and defends belief in the one God revealed through creation, Scripture, and Christ. A convert from paganism, he argued that faith is not opposed to reason and that moral transformation belongs to the reception of truth. His writings contain an early Christian use of language concerning God's triadic life and show the Church engaging surrounding culture while remaining rooted in the biblical account of creation and salvation. Theophilus did not treat knowledge of God as speculation detached from holiness; purity of heart and obedience shape the capacity to see divine truth. His witness invites careful study, charitable explanation of the faith, and humility before revelation. Christian apologetics becomes faithful when it serves conversion, worship, and communion rather than pride or hostility.
dailyPrayer:
Lord Jesus Christ, You have set Your people free through the grace of Your Cross. Keep us from seeking righteousness in outward signs while resisting the conversion of heart that You desire. Deliver us from every attachment that makes us slaves to sin, pride, fear, or human approval. Grant us the faith that works through love, so that our obedience may arise from grateful trust in Your mercy.

Purify what is within us. Where greed, resentment, vanity, or hardness remains hidden, bring the light of Your truth. Teach us to honor the worship and discipline of Your Church with sincere hearts, never using sacred things to conceal a lack of charity. Make us generous toward those in need and ready to receive Your word in humility.

Through the intercession of Saint Theophilus of Antioch, give us a reverent desire to know You through creation, Scripture, and the saving revelation of Christ. May our study lead to worship, our words serve truth with gentleness, and our lives bear witness to the holiness of the Gospel. Amen.
theologicalSynthesis:
Galatians and Luke together reveal that Christian freedom is not permission for self-will, nor is holiness secured by external observance alone. Paul defends the sufficiency of Christ’s grace: no ritual work can replace the saving gift received in faith. Yet this faith is not inert. It becomes visible in love, the form of life given by the Holy Spirit to those united with Christ.

Jesus addresses the corresponding danger of an exterior religion. Ritual purity has meaning only when it expresses a heart turned toward God. The Creator knows both the visible person and the hidden depths of the heart; therefore mercy, generosity, and interior truth belong inseparably to authentic worship. The psalm joins obedience and freedom, teaching that the commandments of God are not contrary to liberation when they are received as the path of communion with him.

Saint Theophilus helps unite these themes. Truth about God calls for both careful confession and moral transformation. Christian proclamation is credible when it arises from humble faith, purified love, and worship of the God who has revealed himself in Christ.
exegesis:
Context: Galatians 5:1-6 stands within Paul’s urgent defense of the Gospel of grace. The apostle has argued that believers are made children of God through faith in Christ, not through adopting the Mosaic Law as the ground of their justification. His concern is not contempt for the Law given by God, nor a rejection of Israel’s sacred history. Rather, Paul opposes the claim that circumcision is necessary for Gentile Christians to belong fully to Christ. If circumcision is accepted as the means by which one is justified, Christ’s saving work is treated as insufficient. Paul therefore summons the Galatians to remain in the freedom bestowed by Christ.

Context: This freedom is profoundly theological. It is deliverance from the condition in which human beings seek to establish righteousness apart from the gift of God. Paul does not describe freedom as independence from the Lord or from the demands of charity. In the verses that follow, he will insist that Christians are called to serve one another through love. Already in today’s passage he identifies the decisive reality: faith working through love. Faith receives Christ and his grace; love manifests the new life that grace creates. Neither a bodily mark nor its absence determines a person’s standing before God. Communion with Christ, expressed in loving obedience, is what matters.

Psalm: Psalm 119 answers Paul’s teaching by showing the proper place of God’s commandments in the life of the faithful. The psalmist does not regard divine instruction as a burden opposed to freedom. He asks for mercy and salvation according to the Lord’s promise, desires that the word of truth remain with him, and hopes in God’s judgments. His obedience is the response of one who has received God’s steadfast love. Thus he can speak of walking freely while seeking the precepts of the Lord. Biblical freedom is not release from truth; it is the capacity, restored by grace, to live according to the truth of God.

Psalm: The psalm also guards against a distorted use of Paul. Since salvation is grace, the commandments cannot be treated as a means of self-justification. Yet grace does not make God’s will irrelevant. The person who trusts the Lord delights in his commandments, meditates upon them, and perseveres in them. Such obedience is filial rather than servile. It flows from confidence in the God who saves. The Church hears this psalm as a prayer for a heart formed by the word, a heart in which doctrine, worship, and conduct belong together. The word on the lips must also take root in the inner person.

Gospel: In Luke 11:37-41, Jesus confronts a religious practice severed from interior conversion. The Pharisee notices that Jesus has not performed the customary washing before the meal. Jesus responds by identifying a deeper uncleanness: greed and wickedness within. His words do not deny that created signs, bodily actions, and ritual observances can serve devotion to God. The difficulty is the pretense that external correctness can stand in place of a heart purified by mercy. The God who made the exterior also made the interior. Nothing hidden is outside his gaze, and no visible act can substitute for conversion.

Gospel: Jesus points toward almsgiving as an expression of a purified interior. Generosity contradicts the grasping disposition he exposes. It directs possessions and desires away from self-enclosure and toward mercy for the neighbor. This teaching harmonizes with Paul’s description of faith active through love. The Gospel does not offer a new external action that earns purity; it calls the person to a merciful disposition before God. When the heart is given to the Lord, acts of worship, fasting, almsgiving, and service can become truthful expressions of communion with him. Without that inward surrender, even religious observance can become a covering for sin.

Saints: Saint Theophilus of Antioch illuminates the unity of truth and holiness in these readings. As a bishop and apologist, he explained the Christian confession of the one God revealed through creation, Scripture, and Christ. Yet his witness, as the surviving account of his teaching indicates, did not separate knowledge of God from moral transformation. This accords with Jesus’ concern for the interior and with Paul’s insistence that faith is living and loving. To speak rightly about God while refusing the purification of the heart would contradict the truth one seeks to defend. Theophilus therefore invites believers to receive revelation humbly, to study it carefully, and to let it lead toward worship and conversion.

Today: The readings call the Church to examine every appearance of religion before the searching gaze of God. We are not saved by external distinctions, ritual accomplishments, or the desire to appear devout. We are saved by Christ, whose grace liberates us for the love of God and neighbor. At the same time, grace truly changes the believer: it forms a heart that seeks God’s commandments, rejects greed and hypocrisy, and gives itself in mercy. Through Saint Theophilus’s intercession, may the Church confess the faith with clarity and charity, rooted in Scripture and open to the God who purifies the whole person. In this way, freedom in Christ becomes the freedom to worship him in truth and to love as he commands.
